corrections.caveats: Single run each, timed by the shell around the whole program, so it includes malloc of 1.6 GB and the fill pass; fill() walks the matrix in row order in both modes, so the measured ratio understates the gap between the two traversals themselves. Compiler flags and CPU not stated and the repo carries no result files. The program accumulates into a signed int, which overflows at this size (about 4e12 expected) and is undefined behaviour in C, though both loops do the same arithmetic. The build is probably unoptimised (no flags in the repo), where the gap is dominated by cache and TLB misses and can differ when a compiler interchanges loops (GCC enables -floop-interchange at -O3). The usage message in main() has a printf format bug (argv[0] passed to the wrong printf) that does not affect the timing. The baseline is a loop order over a raw C array, not one of the category's listed std containers. Tier C: first-party book measurement. corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated. The repo has no build files (no CMakeLists.txt or Makefile at the root or in Chapter10); the README lists only 'GCC, Clang or Visual Studio' for Chapter 1 and no flags.
corrections.caveats: The queue as written in this file is functionally wrong (by reading the source, not compiled or run here): push() writes buf_[(++front_) & 15] while front() reads buf_[tail_ & 15], so front() returns the element pushed one step earlier (the first read is an uninitialised slot) and the last pushed element is never read; the benchmark only passes front() to DoNotOptimize and checks no values, so the timing does not catch it, but the 4.7x is measured on a container that is not yet a correct FIFO. The size check (front_ - tail_ > 16) also lets a 17th element in, overwriting a live slot. state.SetItemsProcessed(32*iterations) counts 32 items per iteration although each iteration pushes and pops 224 ints (32 x 7), so the items/s figures understate real throughput 7x on both sides (the ratio is unaffected). Bounded versus unbounded, so not a drop-in replacement; std::queue<int> uses its default std::deque<int>. Book numbers, compiler, flags and CPU not stated, first-party. Tier C. File opened: Chapter10/08_small_queue.C.
